message.text: Design the consistency model for the shared scene. Two headsets and a laptop mutate the same columns through the Node hub; Hermes keeps appending messages concurrently; clients reconnect over flaky venue Wi-Fi and must never see duplicates or ghost tiles. Be concrete: ordering, idempotency, what may be predicted locally, and how fixture replay loops fit in.

text: The question has three moving
parts: who is allowed to write, how order is defined, and
what a client may show before the server has confirmed
it. Start with the writer.
If both headsets and the laptop could mutate
columns directly we would need
CRDTs or a merge
rule for every field:
position, scroll, tile order. None
of that is necessary if the hub is the single writer:
every client sends a command, the
hub validates it against canonical state, and the
only thing that leaves the hub is an event
with a monotonic sequence number. Order then has one
definition, the server's seq, and
every client that applies events in seq
order converges on the same scene by construction. Hermes
fits the same funnel: the adapter polls the dashboard,
diffs rows, and feeds the same reducer, so
an agent message
and a judge's pipe command are both just events with
a seq. The cost is latency on the headset's
own actions, one round trip through the hub, which
over a tunnel is 100 to
300 ms. That is acceptable for a tile appearing but
not for a hand carrying a tile, so
the carry must be predicted locally; I
will come back to
that. Snapshot versus replay: a joining
client needs the full state once,
then only deltas. The hub keeps a
ring buffer of the last N events;
a client reconnecting with lastSeq inside the buffer
gets the gap replayed,
otherwise a fresh snapshot.
The snapshot must carry the seq it
was taken at so the client can discard any
replayed event with seq <= snapshot.seq. Without that,
a snapshot followed by an overlapping replay
double-applies a message.add and a ghost
tile appears, which is
exactly the bug the question forbids. One
more subtlety: the server must take the
snapshot and record its seq atomically with
respect to the broadcast loop, otherwise an event can
slip between the two and
be neither in the snapshot nor
after it.

The question has three moving parts: who is allowed to write, how order is defined, and what a client may show before the server has confirmed it. Start with the writer. If both headsets and the laptop could mutate columns directly we would need CRDTs or a merge rule for every field: position, scroll, tile order. None of that is necessary if the hub is the single writer: every client sends a command, the hub validates it against canonical state, and the only thing that leaves the hub is an event with a monotonic sequence number. Order then has one definition, the server's seq, and every client that applies events in seq order converges on the same scene by construction. Hermes fits the same funnel: the adapter polls the dashboard, diffs rows, and feeds the same reducer, so an agent message and a judge's pipe command are both just events with a seq. The cost is latency on the headset's own actions, one round trip through the hub, which over a tunnel is 100 to 300 ms. That is acceptable for a tile appearing but not for a hand carrying a tile, so the carry must be predicted locally; I will come back to that. Snapshot versus replay: a joining client needs the full state once, then only deltas. The hub keeps a ring buffer of the last N events; a client reconnecting with lastSeq inside the buffer gets the gap replayed, otherwise a fresh snapshot. The snapshot must carry the seq it was taken at so the client can discard any replayed event with seq <= snapshot.seq. Without that, a snapshot followed by an overlapping replay double-applies a message.add and a ghost tile appears, which is exactly the bug the question forbids. One more subtlety: the server must take the snapshot and record its seq atomically with respect to the broadcast loop, otherwise an event can slip between the two and be neither in the snapshot nor after it.

message.text:
63: ## 2. Transport
64: 
65: - One WebSocket endpoint `/ws`. JSON text frames, one envelope per frame. Binary frames are **not** used (audio travels as base64 inside JSON for simplicity).
66: - Connect sequence: client → `{t:"join", device, name, lastSeq?}`; server → `hello`, then either `snapshot` (new client or gap too large) or a replay of `event` frames with `seq > lastSeq`, then live frames.
67: - Every state change is a server `event` with a monotonic `seq`. Clients never mutate shared state locally except the object they are carrying (local prediction); they send a command and apply the resulting events like everyone else.
68: - Per-viewer local view state (summon, scroll offset, detail plane, LOD) is never sent.

text: Idempotency. A monotonic seq handles
ordering but not duplicates across a reconnect, because
the client may have applied events the server now replays
again. Two layers. First, the client
drops any event with seq <= its lastApplied.
Second, and more robust, every
entity carries a stable id: Session.id from
Hermes, Message.id from the
Hermes row id (with
:r for the reasoning split
and :callId for each
tool call), tool.start
and tool.complete keyed by callId. A
message.add for an id the store
already has is an upsert, not an
append, so the tile count cannot drift even if
the seq check is bypassed at a snapshot boundary.
message.delta is the one non-idempotent event: appending
the same chunk twice corrupts the text.
So deltas are best effort, and message.complete
carries the full text
and replaces the buffer; a client that
missed or doubled a delta heals at
completion. That is also why the
fixture format puts the final text in message.complete.
Layout conflicts: two people
can drag the same base
at once. The hub
applies layout.move in arrival order
and emits layout.colu
mn with by: clientId; the
last event wins and every
client animates to it. The dragging client
ignores incoming layout.column for the
column it is carrying until it releases,
then snaps to the authoritative position. Forks:
the child gets a fresh id minted by the server,
never by the client, so two clients forking the same
column at the same moment
produce two children, not one
collision. Pipes: the
composed user message
is created by the hub with via: pipe and from:
{sessionId, messageId};
the source tile is never mutated. Removal:
session.remove is a tombstone
event the client applies by fading, and
the server keeps the id in a tombstone set for the ring
buffer's lifetime so a late message.add for a removed
session is dropped rather
than resurrecting the column.

First, the client drops any event with seq <= its lastApplied. Second, and more robust, every entity carries a stable id: Session.id from Hermes, Message.id from the Hermes row id (with :r for the reasoning split and :callId for each tool call), tool.start and tool.complete keyed by callId. A message.add for an id the store already has is an upsert, not an append, so the tile count cannot drift even if the seq check is bypassed at a snapshot boundary. message.delta is the one non-idempotent event: appending the same chunk twice corrupts the text. So deltas are best effort, and message.complete carries the full text and replaces the buffer; a client that missed or doubled a delta heals at completion. That is also why the fixture format puts the final text in message.complete. Layout conflicts: two people can drag the same base at once. The hub applies layout.move in arrival order and emits layout.column with by: clientId; the last event wins and every client animates to it. The dragging client ignores incoming layout.column for the column it is carrying until it releases, then snaps to the authoritative position. Forks: the child gets a fresh id minted by the server, never by the client, so two clients forking the same column at the same moment produce two children, not one collision. Pipes: the composed user message is created by the hub with via: pipe and from: {sessionId, messageId}; the source tile is never mutated. Removal: session.remove is a tombstone event the client applies by fading, and the server keeps the id in a tombstone set for the ring buffer's lifetime so a late message.add for a removed session is dropped rather than resurrecting the column.
What may be predicted locally? Exactly one thing:
the object the viewer's own
hand is carrying — the tile copy during a
pipe, the ghost column during a fork, the
base during a move. These are
per-viewer view state until release; on
release the client sends the command and keeps
showing the predicted result until the hub's event
arrives, then reconciles,
usually a no-op,
sometimes a 400 ms slide to
the authoritative spot.
Everything else —
summon, scroll offset,
detail plane, LOD — is purely local
and never sent, so it cannot conflict.
Presence is the opposite extreme: it
is sent at 10 Hz but it is not state,
it is a sample; it goes through the
hub without a seq and is not in the ring buffer, because
replaying old head poses after a reconnect would be
nonsense. Fixture replay loops are a special case of
idempotency: when all files are exhausted the
replayer re-emits the same messages with an id
suffix so the store sees new entities and the
columns keep growing;
without the suffix the upserts
would be no-ops and the loop would be
invisible. Reset is a
server-side event sequence:
session.remove for judge-made
forks, layout.column back to the
file, then a fresh
snapshot to everyone; seq keeps increasing —
we never rewind seq, we only change state. Clock: event
ts is the server's receive
time and is used for display only;
ordering never depends on it, so
clock skew between a
headset and the laptop is harmless. Finally the
status machine: status is derived on
the server from the
newest row and emitted as
session.status, so no client
guesses the ring colour from
its own partial view,
and a reconnecting client gets the current colour
from the snapshot rather than replaying a minute of
transitions.

These are per-viewer view state until release; on release the client sends the command and keeps showing the predicted result until the hub's event arrives, then reconciles, usually a no-op, sometimes a 400 ms slide to the authoritative spot. Everything else — summon, scroll offset, detail plane, LOD — is purely local and never sent, so it cannot conflict. Presence is the opposite extreme: it is sent at 10 Hz but it is not state, it is a sample; it goes through the hub without a seq and is not in the ring buffer, because replaying old head poses after a reconnect would be nonsense. Finally the status machine: status is derived on the server from the newest row and emitted as session.status, so no client guesses the ring colour from its own partial view, and a reconnecting client gets the current colour from the snapshot rather than replaying a minute of transitions.

text:
**Consistency model for the shared scene**

1. **Single
writer.** The hub owns canonical state.
Clients send commands; the hub
validates, mutates and emits events
with a monotonic `seq`. Hermes rows enter
through the same reducer. Convergence follows from

applying events in `seq` order.
2. **Resume without
ghosts.** `join {lastSeq}`: if the gap is
inside the 5000-event ring buffer, replay it; otherwise
send `snapshot {seq}`. Clients drop any event with
`seq <= lastApplied` and treat
`snapshot.seq` as the new floor. Snapshot and its seq

are taken atomically.
3. **Idempotent
entities.** Every session, message and
tool call carries a stable id (Hermes row id, `:r`,
`:callId`). `message.add` is an upsert;
`tool.start`/`tool.complete` key on `callId`;
`session.remove` leaves a tombstone so late

adds are dropped.
4. **Deltas
are best effort.** `message.delta` appends;
`message.complete` carries the full text and
replaces the buffer. Lost or doubled

chunks heal at completion.
5. **Conflicts resolve
by `seq`.** `layout.column` is
last-writer-wins; the dragging client ignores
incoming moves for the object it holds until
release. Forks and pipes get

server-minted ids.
6. **Local prediction = the carried
object only.** Tile copy, ghost column, dragged
base. Summon, scroll, detail plane and LOD are
per-viewer and never sent. Presence is sampled at 10 Hz,

unsequenced, not buffered.
7.
**Fixture loops and reset**
stay inside the model: re-emitted ids get a loop suffix,
reset is an ordinary event sequence plus
a snapshot; `seq` never rewinds. `ts`

is display only.

Invariant to test: after

**Consistency model for the shared scene**

1. **Single writer.** The hub owns canonical state. Clients send commands; the hub validates, mutates and emits events with a monotonic `seq`. Hermes rows enter through the same reducer. Convergence follows from applying events in `seq` order.
2. **Resume without ghosts.** `join {lastSeq}`: if the gap is inside the 5000-event ring buffer, replay it; otherwise send `snapshot {seq}`. Clients drop any event with `seq <= lastApplied` and treat `snapshot.seq` as the new floor. Snapshot and its seq are taken atomically.
3. **Idempotent entities.** Every session, message and tool call carries a stable id (Hermes row id, `:r`, `:callId`). `message.add` is an upsert; `tool.start`/`tool.complete` key on `callId`; `session.remove` leaves a tombstone so late adds are dropped.
4. **Deltas are best effort.** `message.delta` appends; `message.complete` carries the full text and replaces the buffer. Lost or doubled chunks heal at completion.
5. **Conflicts resolve by `seq`.** `layout.column` is last-writer-wins; the dragging client ignores incoming moves for the object it holds until release. Forks and pipes get server-minted ids.
6. **Local prediction = the carried object only.** Tile copy, ghost column, dragged base. Summon, scroll, detail plane and LOD are per-viewer and never sent. Presence is sampled at 10 Hz, unsequenced, not buffered.
7. **Fixture loops and reset** stay inside the model: re-emitted ids get a loop suffix, reset is an ordinary event sequence plus a snapshot; `seq` never rewinds. `ts` is display only.

Invariant to test: after any sequence of disconnects, `store == reduce(snapshot, events.filter(e => e.seq > snapshot.seq))` on every client.

message.text: What about the Hermes side? The adapter polls at 1 Hz and Hermes can compact history. Does that break anything?

message.summary: Compaction is the case I had not covered.

text: Compaction is the case I
had not covered. Hermes can rewrite history: it marks
rows compacted and inserts a
summary row, so a row
id the adapter already emitted may vanish
from the latest page while a new row
appears in the middle of the
transcript. Polling the latest 60 rows and
diffing by row id
handles additions and simply never sees a removal, which is
the right default for a
display: a tile that was shown stays shown,
and the summary row is
appended as a system
message. If we ever want
removals we need include_compacted plus a
per-message tombstone, which the protocol
does not have; add
message.remove as an optional kind later rather
than deleting anything locally on
a hunch. The 1 Hz poll also means
the live status lags up to
a second behind the dashboard, which is why status
should be derived
from the newest row plus a 10 s liveness
window, not from is_active alone, whose
300 s window would keep a
ring green for
minutes after the agent went quiet. And the optional
/api/ws stream must be treated as a hint layer on
the same ids: message.delta onto <sid>:live, which
the poller's message.comple
te with the real row id then supersedes, so the stream
can drop out at any time
and the poller still converges. Nothing in
the model changes; the
adapter is just another client of the
reducer with a slower clock.

Compaction is the case I had not covered. Hermes can rewrite history: it marks rows compacted and inserts a summary row, so a row id the adapter already emitted may vanish from the latest page while a new row appears in the middle of the transcript. Polling the latest 60 rows and diffing by row id handles additions and simply never sees a removal, which is the right default for a display: a tile that was shown stays shown, and the summary row is appended as a system message. If we ever want removals we need include_compacted plus a per-message tombstone, which the protocol does not have; add message.remove as an optional kind later rather than deleting anything locally on a hunch. The 1 Hz poll also means the live status lags up to a second behind the dashboard, which is why status should be derived from the newest row plus a 10 s liveness window, not from is_active alone, whose 300 s window would keep a ring green for minutes after the agent went quiet. And the optional /api/ws stream must be treated as a hint layer on the same ids: message.delta onto <sid>:live, which the poller's message.complete with the real row id then supersedes, so the stream can drop out at any time and the poller still converges. Status should come from the newest row plus a 10 s liveness window rather than `is_active`. The optional `/api/ws` stream is a hint layer on the same ids that the poller's `message.complete` supersedes, so it can drop out without affecting convergence.
